a: Apollonius son of Menestheus, the governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, was adding
p: Swete prints a guess by Hort. The two codices say Apollonius was 'raging', as the KJV has it.

readings.w: Swete's text, following a conjecture by F. J. A. Hort ("son of Menestheus", as in 4:21)
readings.plain: Apollonius son of Menestheus, the governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, was adding

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Venetus (V), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("Apollonius... did rage, and increase Simon's malice") and the Vulgate (Apollonium insanire) give this sense
readings.orig: Μενεσθεως coniec Ηορτ] μαινεσθαι εως A μ. ως V
readings.en: Apollonius raging, so as to increase (Simon's wickedness)
readings.plain: Apollonius, the governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, was raging and adding

why: Both codices have a verb, mainesthai, 'to rage', where Swete prints a name. Swete's apparatus records only that the reading is Hort's conjecture. It rests on the closeness of the letters of 'raging until' (MAINESTHAIHEŌS) to 'of Menestheus' (MENESTHEŌS), the name of Apollonius's father in 4:21, and on the clause reading badly without a name. Against the conjecture, 3:5 calls the governor 'Apollonius son of Thrasaeus', so Hort's correction may give him the wrong father. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's printed text, the base of this site, but the manuscripts' 'raging' is old and was read by the Latin and the KJV.
b: Swete's apparatus writes Hort's name in Greek letters by a digitizing slip ("Ηορτ").

a: the best men among us
p: Alexandrinus speaks of 'the best among us'; Venetus, the KJV and the Vulgate have 'the young men in training'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: the best of those among us
readings.plain: the best men among us

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("the chief young men") and the Vulgate (optimos quosque epheborum) follow this text
readings.plain: the best of the young men in training

why: The two readings differ by a few letters (eph' hēmōn, ephēbōn). Venetus's 'ephebes', the youths enrolled in the gymnasium's training corps (4:9), fits the context well and is printed by many editors. But Alexandrinus makes sense too, in the voice of a Jewish writer ('the best of our people'), so the Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: the overwhelming impurity of Jason
p: Alexandrinus has 'purity', which cannot be right; Swete prints Venetus's 'impurity'.

readings.w: Swete's text, from Codex Venetus (V)
readings.plain: the overwhelming impurity of Jason

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: the overwhelming purity of Jason

why: A scribe of Alexandrinus dropped two letters (an-), turning the writer's charge into praise. The sentence calls Jason ungodly in the same breath, so A's reading is a slip. Swete prints the reading of Venetus here, and the Plain English Translation follows him.

a: But the men who carried the money asked that it not be used for a sacrifice,
t: A shorter and a longer text
p: Alexandrinus says the envoys asked that the money not go to the sacrifice. Venetus and the KJV add 'but for another expense'. With 4:20.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἃς καὶ ἠξίωσαν οἱ παρακομίζοντες μὴ χρῆσθαι εἰς θυσίαν
readings.en: which the bearers asked not to use for a sacrifice
readings.plain: But the men who carried the money asked that it not be used for a sacrifice,

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("which even the bearers thereof thought fit not to bestow upon the sacrifice, because it was not convenient, but to be reserved for other charges") and the Vulgate (quia non oporteret, sed in alios sumptus eas deputari) have a text like this
readings.orig: θυσιαν 2° + εις ετεραν δε καταθεσθαι δαπανην V
readings.en: ...to use for a sacrifice, but to lay it out for another expense
readings.plain: But the men who carried the money asked that it not be used for a sacrifice, since that was not fitting, but that it be set aside for another expense.

why: Alexandrinus runs straight on into 4:20 ('...but, because of the circumstances, for fitting out warships'), and makes good sense. Venetus smooths the passage with an added clause; the KJV's 'because it was not convenient' is found in the Latin (quia non oporteret) but not in Swete's two codices. The Plain English Translation keeps the shorter base text.
b: The two entries for 4:19 and 4:20 go together.

a: but, because of the circumstances, for fitting out warships.
t: Who decided where the money went?
p: Venetus and the KJV explain that the money went to Heracles for the sender's sake, but to the ships because of the bearers. With 4:19.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἕνεκα δὲ τῶν παρόντων εἰς τὰς τῶν τριηρέων κατασκευάς
readings.en: but on account of the present (circumstances) for the fitting out of the triremes
readings.plain: but, because of the circumstances, for fitting out warships.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus ("br" is probably a digitizing slip for "pr", 'added before'); the KJV ("This money then, in regard of the sender, was appointed to Hercules' sacrifice; but because of the bearers thereof, it was employed to the making of gallies") and the Vulgate follow a text like this
readings.orig: 20 ενεκα] br επεισε δε ταυτα δια μεν τον αποστειλαντα εις την Ηρακλεους θυσια V | παροντων] παρακομιζοντων V
readings.en: it fell out that this (money), because of the sender, (went) to the sacrifice of Heracles, but because of those who carried it, to the triremes
readings.plain: So the money was meant for the sacrifice to Heracles because of the man who sent it, but it went to fitting out warships because of the men who carried it.

why: Venetus's longer text spells out a contrast between the sender and the bearers, and reads 'the bearers' (parakomizontōn) for A's 'the present (things)' (parontōn). It looks like an explanation of the harder short text. The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus, where tōn parontōn most likely means 'the circumstances', though it could mean 'those present'.
b: The two entries for 4:19 and 4:20 go together.

a: was cheated out of it by another
p: Swete's text repeats the verb of 4:7, 'got by fraud'; Alexandrinus and the KJV have 'undermined'.

readings.w: Swete's text, with Venetus
readings.plain: was cheated out of it by another

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("being undermined by another") gives this sense
readings.plain: was undermined by another

why: Swete corrects Alexandrinus here. His text gives the same verb twice, 'who had cheated his brother ... cheated by another', a play the writer likes (4:7). Alexandrinus's hyponomeutheis, 'undermined (as by a mine)', differs by a few letters and gives the KJV its 'undermined'. The meaning is close.

a: reported it
p: Alexandrinus says Onias 'reported' the theft; Venetus, the KJV and the Vulgate say he 'reproved' or 'exposed' Menelaus.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: reported it

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("he reproved him") and the Vulgate (arguebat eum) follow this text
readings.plain: exposed him

why: The two Greek verbs look much alike (apēnegken, apēlegchen). Venetus's 'exposed, rebuked' is the more vivid reading and many editors print it, but Alexandrinus's verb can mean 'brought back word, reported', which fits Onias sending word of the theft to the authorities. The sense is close either way: Onias made Menelaus's crime known.

a: Onias had been killed for no reason
p: Swete prints Venetus's passive; Alexandrinus has an active verb, '(that) he had killed Onias'.

readings.w: Swete's text, from Codex Venetus (V)
readings.plain: Onias had been killed for no reason

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: he had killed Onias for no reason

why: Alexandrinus's finite verb does not fit the sentence, so Swete follows Venetus. The digital apparatus spells Venetus's word 'απεκτοοησθαι', a typing slip for ἀπεκτονῆσθαι. The sense is the same either way.

a: a man far along in years and just as far in ignorance
p: Venetus makes Auranus 'a tyrant' advanced 'in folly'; the KJV has 'folly', the Vulgate both.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: προβεβηκότος τὴν ἡλικίαν, οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ τὴν ἄγνοιαν
readings.en: advanced in age and no less in ignorance
readings.plain: a man far along in years and just as far in ignorance

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("a man far gone in years, and no less in folly") has 'folly'; the Vulgate has both (duce quodam tyranno, ætate pariter et dementia provecto)
readings.orig: Αυρανου] +τυραννου V | την αγνοιαν] τη ανοια V
readings.en: Auranus, a tyrant, advanced in age and no less in folly
readings.plain: a tyrant far along in years and just as far in folly

why: The difference is small: agnoia 'ignorance' against anoia 'folly', one letter apart. Venetus also calls Auranus a 'tyrant'. The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus.

a: spears in crowds
p: Alexandrinus has 'masses of toils', which does not fit a list of weapons; the Plain English Translation follows Venetus, 'masses of spears'.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("multitude of pikes") follows this text
readings.plain: spears in crowds

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: great labors

why: Kamatōn ('toils, labors') and kamakōn ('shafts, spear-shafts') differ by one letter. In a list of swords, shields and missiles only the second makes sense, so the Plain English Translation departs from the base text here. The Vulgate (galeatorum multitudinem, 'a crowd of men in helmets') may reflect yet another reading.

a: He was shut in by Aretas
p: The Greek says Jason was 'shut in' by Aretas; the KJV has 'accused before Aretas'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; no variant in Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate agrees (conclusus ab Areta)
readings.plain: He was shut in by Aretas

readings.w: The KJV ("being accused before Aretas"), perhaps from a printed Greek reading enklētheis, 'accused' (not in Swete's apparatus)
readings.plain: He was accused before Aretas

why: Swete's codices and the Latin all read enkleistheis, 'shut in, confined'. The KJV's 'accused' would come from enklētheis, a very similar word; the editions behind the KJV are not reported here, so the reading is given only as the KJV's English. The phrase pros Aretan is odd with either verb, and some scholars suspect the text is damaged.

a: had no part in the rites of his fathers' law
t: His fathers' law, or his fathers' tomb?
p: Alexandrinus says Jason had no share in 'the ancestral law' of burial; Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV say 'the tomb of his fathers'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: nor did he share in ancestral law
readings.plain: had no part in the rites of his fathers' law

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (neque patrio sepulchro participans) and the KJV ("nor sepulchre with his fathers") follow this text
readings.en: nor did he share in the ancestral tomb
readings.plain: had no part in the tomb of his fathers

why: Taphou 'tomb' is the easier reading and many editors print it, but Alexandrinus's nomou 'law' makes sense: Jason, who broke the ancestral laws (4:11; 5:8), was denied the burial they require. The book likes such measure-for-measure endings. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: The gifts many kings had set up
p: Alexandrinus says 'many kings'; Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV say 'other kings'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: the things set up by many kings
readings.plain: The gifts many kings had set up

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (ab aliis regibus et civitatibus, 'by other kings and cities') and the KJV ("by other kings") follow this text
readings.orig: υπο πολλων] πολλ sup ras Aa υπ αλλων V
readings.en: the things set up by others (kings)
readings.plain: The gifts other kings had set up

why: In Alexandrinus the word 'many' was written over an erasure by a corrector (Aᵃ). Venetus's 'by others' contrasts these kings with Antiochus. The difference is small; the Plain English Translation keeps Swete's printed text.
b: The KJV's "he gave them away" at the end of the verse renders the Greek synsyrōn, 'sweeping together', loosely; it is not a different reading.

a: Overtaken when the Almighty was angry
p: Both codices say the place was 'overtaken' in God's anger; the Latin and the KJV have 'forsaken'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Venetus has the same verb, misspelled, corrected by a later hand
readings.orig: ὁ καταληφθεὶς ἐν τῇ τοῦ παντοκράτορος ὀργῇ
readings.en: the one overtaken in the Almighty's anger
readings.plain: Overtaken when the Almighty was angry

readings.w: Later editions read καταλειφθείς; the Vulgate (qui derelictus in ira Dei omnipotentis est) and the KJV ("as it was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty") give this sense
readings.orig: qui derelictus in ira Dei omnipotentis est
readings.en: the one forsaken in the Almighty's anger
readings.plain: Forsaken when the Almighty was angry

why: Swete's apparatus reports only Venetus's misspelling (καταλημφθης V* (-ληφθεις Vᵃ)), so both codices have the verb 'seize, overtake'. 'Left, forsaken' (kataleiphtheis) differs by one letter and fits the next clause, 'set upright again'; many modern editions print it. The Plain English Translation keeps the codices.

a: dry land fit for ships
p: Swete prints 'the land navigable'; Alexandrinus has a slip, 'the first'.

readings.w: Swete's text, with Venetus; the KJV ("to make the land navigable")
readings.plain: dry land fit for ships

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: the first

why: Alexandrinus's tēn prōtēn makes no sense with what follows ('and the sea passable on foot'); Swete corrects it from Venetus.

a: twenty-two thousand
p: Venetus gives Apollonius 21,000 men; Alexandrinus, the Vulgate and the KJV have 22,000.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the Vulgate and the KJV agree
readings.plain: twenty-two thousand

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.orig: τοις δισχιλιοις] προς τοις χιλιοις V
readings.plain: twenty-one thousand

why: A small difference in the number. The Plain English Translation follows the base text, which the Latin and the KJV share.

a: he posted large forces there
p: Alexandrinus says Apollonius 'set up' large numbers in the city; Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV say he 'laid low' great crowds.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: he posted large forces there

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (ingentem multitudinem peremit) and the KJV ("slew great multitudes") follow this text
readings.plain: he laid great crowds low

why: The verbs differ by two letters (katestēsen, katestrōsen). Venetus's 'laid low' continues the killing at the start of the verse, and most translations follow it. Alexandrinus can be read as 'he stationed large forces', which fits the garrison the king left behind (1 Maccabees 1:33–34). The Plain English Translation keeps the base text, since it makes sense.

a: withdrew
p: Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV add that Judas withdrew 'into the wilderness'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: withdrew

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (secesserat in desertum locum) and the KJV ("withdrew himself into the wilderness") follow this text
readings.plain: withdrew into the wilderness

why: The added words make explicit what 'the mountains' already imply. The Plain English Translation keeps the shorter base text.

a: an elderly Athenian
t: An Athenian, or a man of Antioch?
p: The Greek has 'an old Athenian'; the Vulgate and the Douay have 'an old man of Antioch'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; no variant in Swete's apparatus; the KJV agrees ("an old man of Athens")
readings.plain: an elderly Athenian

readings.w: The Vulgate (senem quemdam Antiochenum) and the Douay ("a certain old man of Antioch")
readings.en: a certain old man of Antioch
readings.plain: an elderly man of Antioch

why: All of Swete's Greek witnesses read 'Athenian'. The Latin 'Antiochene' may come from a Greek copy that read Antiocheus, or from a translator who found an Athenian odd. On whether gerōn is 'old man', a member of a council, or a name (Geron), see the note.

a: who amused themselves with prostitutes
p: Both codices read 'others'; Swete prints a correction to 'courtesans' and asks whether 'companions' is meant.

readings.w: Swete's text (Swete's note asks whether ἑταίρων, 'companions', is meant)
readings.plain: who amused themselves with prostitutes

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Venetus (V), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: who amused themselves with others

why: Without accents the two words differ by one letter: hetairōn ('courtesans', or 'companions') and heterōn ('others'). The Latin (cum meretricibus) and the KJV ("with harlots") read 'prostitutes', and so does the next clause, about women in the sacred courts. Swete prints hetairōn, 'courtesans', against the codices' heterōn, 'others'; the query in his note, '(? ἑταίρων)', asks only whether the accent should make it 'companions'. The Plain English Translation follows his text.

a: the feasts of the fathers
p: The Greek has 'ancestral feasts'; the KJV text has 'ancient fasts'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; no variant in Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate agrees (dies solemnes patrii)
readings.plain: the feasts of the fathers

readings.w: The KJV ("ancient fasts")
readings.plain: the ancient fasts

why: Heortai are feasts, not fasts, in every witness Swete reports and in the Latin. The KJV's 'fasts', and its 'fast of Bacchus' in 6:7, look like errors in its English, since 'feast' and 'fast' are easily confused in print. They are listed so a reader comparing the KJV sees the difference.

a: the festival of Dionysus
t: The festival of Dionysus, or a "fast"?
p: The KJV text calls it 'the fast of Bacchus'; the Greek has 'the festival of the Dionysia'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the Vulgate agrees (cum Liberi sacra celebrarentur)
readings.plain: the festival of Dionysus

readings.w: The KJV ("when the fast of Bacchus was kept")
readings.plain: the fast of Bacchus

why: Bacchus is the Latin name of Dionysus. The Dionysia were feasts of wine and processions, not fasts; see the entry on 6:6.

a: At Ptolemy's suggestion
t: Ptolemy, or the people of Ptolemais?
p: Swete's text names Ptolemy as the one who proposed the decree; Alexandrinus and the Latin may point to the city of Ptolemais.

readings.w: Swete's text; Alexandrinus differs (see below)
readings.plain: At Ptolemy's suggestion

readings.w: The Vulgate (suggerentibus Ptolemæis) and the Douay ("by the suggestion of the Ptolemeans")
readings.plain: At the suggestion of the people of Ptolemais

why: Swete's apparatus shows that Alexandrinus has the singular polis with a stop after Ptolemaiou ('πολις Πτολεμαιου· (sic) A'), which can be read 'the neighboring Greek city of Ptolemy[ais]', close to the Latin; Venetus first wrote 'Ptolemy' in the nominative. The Latin's plural points to a Greek text that named the citizens of Ptolemais (Acco), the nearest large Greek city, and some modern editors and translations adopt that. The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, in which Ptolemy is most likely the governor of 4:45 and 8:8.

a: pig's meat
p: Both codices read 'a son's meat', a copying slip; Swete prints 'pig's meat'.

readings.w: Swete's text; the KJV ("swine’s flesh") and the Vulgate (carnem porcinam)
readings.plain: pig's meat

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Venetus (V), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: a son's meat

why: Hyeion ('of swine') and huion ('son') sounded alike in later Greek, and both codices wrote the second. The sense requires pork, as in 6:21 and 7:1. Swete corrects the codices; see also 7:1.

a: called on him to bring in meat
p: Alexandrinus has a verb that can mean 'call on, appeal to'; Venetus has 'urged', as the KJV and the Latin take it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: called on him to bring in meat

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("besought him") and the Vulgate (rogabant) give this sense
readings.plain: urged him to bring in meat

why: Enkalein usually means 'to accuse', which does not fit; here it seems to mean 'to call on, press'. Venetus's parekaloun, 'urged', is the easier word. The meaning is close, and the Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: of the distinguished way of life he had gained
t: His way of life, or his gray hair?
p: Alexandrinus praises Eleazar's 'acquired and distinguished way of life'; Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV have his 'gray hair'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: his acquired and distinguished way of life
readings.plain: of the distinguished way of life he had gained

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (ingenitæ nobilitatis canitiem) and the KJV ("the honour of his gray head, whereon was come") follow this text
readings.orig: και επι- φανους πολιτειας] επιφανιας (-νειας Vᵃ) και της πολιας V
readings.en: the distinction of his gray hair
readings.plain: of the gray hair he had earned with distinction

why: Politeias ('way of life, citizenship') and polias ('gray hair') look alike. 'Gray hair' suits an old man and is printed by many editors; 'way of life' is the book's word for the ancestral constitution (4:11; 8:17) and fits Eleazar's praise just as well. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: a short and passing bit of life
p: Swete prints a correction, 'momentary'; Alexandrinus has 'untimely' and Venetus 'pure'.

readings.w: Swete's text; the KJV ("a little time and a moment longer") gives this sense
readings.plain: a short and passing bit of life

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Venetus (V), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: this short and untimely (A) / pure (V) living
readings.plain: a short and untimely bit of life

why: Akariaios, 'lasting a moment', fits 'short'. The codices' akaireon, 'untimely', and akeraion, 'pure, unharmed', are near in spelling; the Vulgate's corruptibilis vitæ may render a form of the second. Swete's correction gives the clearest sense.

a: he went at once to the torture frame
t: He went, or he was dragged?
p: Alexandrinus says Eleazar 'went' to the rack; Venetus and the Vulgate say he 'was dragged'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV agrees ("he went to the torment")
readings.en: he went at once to the rack
readings.plain: he went at once to the torture frame

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (confestim ad supplicium trahebatur)
readings.en: he was dragged at once to the rack
readings.plain: he was dragged at once to the torture frame

why: Alexandrinus agrees with 6:19, where Eleazar goes 'of his own free will'. The Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: the forbidden pork
p: Alexandrinus and the first hand of Venetus write 'sons' meat', the same slip as 6:18.

readings.w: Swete's text; the KJV ("swine’s flesh") and the Vulgate (carnes porcinas)
readings.plain: the forbidden pork

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and the first hand of Codex Venetus (V*), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: the forbidden meat of sons

why: See 6:18. The sense requires pork; Swete corrects the codices.

a: Are you going to question us and find out from us?
p: Alexandrinus has a challenge, 'Are you going to question us?'; Venetus adds 'what', as the KJV and the Vulgate have it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: are you about to ask and learn from us?
readings.plain: Are you going to question us and find out from us?

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("What wouldest thou ask or learn of us?") and the Vulgate (Quid quæris) follow this text
readings.en: what are you about to ask and learn from us?
readings.plain: What are you going to ask us and find out from us?

why: Venetus puts tí, 'what', before the verb. Without it the brother does not offer information; he challenges the king's right to question them at all. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: useless in the rest of his body
p: Alexandrinus says he was useless 'in the rest' of his body; Venetus has 'wholly', as the KJV and the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἄχρηστον δὲ αὐτὸν τοῖς λοιποῖς γενόμενον
readings.plain: useless in the rest of his body

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("maimed in all his members") and the Vulgate (per omnia inutilis) give this sense
readings.plain: useless in every limb

why: After his tongue, scalp, hands and feet were cut away (7:4), Alexandrinus says the rest of his body was useless; Venetus's holois, 'wholly', is the simpler word. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: From Heaven I have these
p: Alexandrinus reads 'these have been called from heaven', which makes little sense; the Plain English Translation follows Venetus, 'I have obtained these from heaven'.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (E cælo ista possideo) and the KJV ("These I had from heaven") follow this text
readings.en: I have acquired these from heaven
readings.plain: From Heaven I have these

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: from heaven these have been called
readings.plain: From Heaven these were called into being

why: Keklētai and kektēmai differ in two letters. 'I have them from Heaven' matches the rest of the sentence ('I hope to receive them back'), and the Latin and the KJV read it. A defender of Alexandrinus could take 'called' as 'called into being' (compare Romans 4:17), but that sense is strained here. This is a departure from the base text.

a: to pass from among men
p: Alexandrinus has 'to depart from among men'; Venetus has 'at the hands of men', as the KJV and the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: to pass from among men

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("being put to death by men") and the Vulgate (ab hominibus morti datos) give this sense
readings.en: departing (life) at the hands of men
readings.plain: to die at men's hands

why: Apo and hyp' differ by a letter or two. Alexandrinus contrasts human life with the hopes God gives; Venetus stresses that the death is men's doing. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: Do not go on deceiving yourself
p: Alexandrinus has 'do not be deceived further'; Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV have 'in vain'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: Do not go on deceiving yourself

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (Noli frustra errare) and the KJV ("Be not deceived without cause") follow this text
readings.en: do not be deceived in vain
readings.plain: Do not deceive yourself for nothing

why: Mallon 'more, further' and matēn 'in vain' are both possible. Venetus's phrase is the more idiomatic Greek and many translations follow it, but Alexandrinus makes good sense. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: The mother was good beyond all measure
p: Alexandrinus calls the mother 'good'; Venetus 'marvelous', as the KJV and the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: The mother was good beyond all measure

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("the mother was marvellous above all") and the Vulgate (mater mirabilis) follow this text
readings.plain: The mother was marvelous beyond all measure

why: Alexandrinus repeats agathē, 'good', in the next phrase ('worth good remembrance'), a play the writer likes; Venetus avoids the repetition. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.

a: quivering with hopes that come to nothing
p: Swete's φρυττόμενος is a rare form; Venetus has φρυαττόμενος, 'snorting, insolent', the KJV's 'puffed up'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: quivering with hopes that come to nothing

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("puffed up with uncertain hopes") gives this sense; the Vulgate has inflammatus, 'inflamed'
readings.plain: insolent with hopes that come to nothing

why: Phryattesthai is used of a horse that snorts and prances, and so of insolent men; it is the easier reading. Alexandrinus's phryttomenos is otherwise hardly known. The Plain English Translation takes it as a by-form meaning 'excited, quivering' and keeps the base text, but Venetus's sense, 'insolent', may well be what the writer meant.

a: have now fallen under God's covenant of ever-flowing life
p: The codices say the brothers have 'fallen under' God's covenant of ever-flowing life; Hort's conjecture, followed in many modern versions, makes them 'drink' of it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the Vulgate (sub testamento æternæ vitæ effecti sunt) and the KJV ("are dead under God's covenant of everlasting life") read the same verb
readings.orig: ἀενάου ζωῆς ὑπὸ διαθήκην θεοῦ πεπτώκασιν
readings.en: of ever-flowing life, under God's covenant, they have fallen
readings.plain: have now fallen under God's covenant of ever-flowing life

readings.w: A conjecture by F. J. A. Hort, reported in Swete's apparatus
readings.en: they have drunk (of ever-flowing life), under God's covenant
readings.plain: have now drunk of ever-flowing life, under God's covenant

why: Peptōkasin ('have fallen') and pepōkasin ('have drunk') differ by one letter. 'Ever-flowing' (aenaos) is a word for springs and rivers, which makes 'drunk' attractive. But every witness has 'fallen', which can mean that the brothers have died and now stand under God's covenant promise of life. The Plain English Translation keeps the manuscripts.

a: my body and my life
t: Body and life, or body and fortune?
p: Alexandrinus has 'body and fortune'; the Plain English Translation follows Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV, 'body and life (soul)'.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (animam et corpus meum) and the KJV ("my body and life") follow this text
readings.plain: my body and my life

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: my body and my fortune

why: Psychēn and tychēn differ in one letter. 'Body and soul' is a fixed pair (compare 14:38, where Razis 'staked body and soul on Judaism'), and 'fortune' is hard to explain as an offering. This is a departure from the base text.

a: I call, as they did, on God
p: Alexandrinus has the plural, 'calling', which takes in the brothers; Venetus and the Latin have the singular.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: I call, as they did, on God

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the Vulgate (invocans Deum) and the KJV ("beseeching God") give this sense
readings.plain: I call on God

why: The plural is awkward after 'I hand over', but it fits the sentence's 'like my brothers': the youngest speaks for all seven. Venetus smooths it to the singular. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text by adding 'as they did'.

a: to stop the anger of the Almighty
p: Alexandrinus asks God 'to stop' his anger in the martyrs; Venetus, the Latin and the KJV say the anger 'may cease'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: (calling on God) to stop the Almighty's anger
readings.plain: to stop the anger of the Almighty

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("the wrath of the Almighty ... may cease") and the Vulgate (desinet Omnipotentis ira) give this sense
readings.en: (that) the Almighty's anger may come to a stand
readings.plain: may the anger of the Almighty come to a stop

why: Stēsai, 'to stop (something)', depends on 'calling on God' in 7:37: the brothers ask God to end his anger. Venetus's stēnai, 'to stand still', makes the anger simply cease in them, which the Latin and the KJV follow. The difference matters for how the martyrs' deaths work (see the note and the card): in Alexandrinus God is asked to stop his anger. The Plain English Translation keeps the base text.
